subject: Biology
title: Natural Killer Cells
description: A 60-second lesson on Natural Killer Cells.

hook.text: Natural killer cells don't wait for instructions. They find infected or cancerous cells and destroy them.

buildup.text: NK cells patrol the body, checking every cell for distress signals on their surface.

discovery.text: Healthy cells display MHC-I molecules—an 'I'm normal' flag. Missing flags trigger NK cell attack.

twist.text: Cancer cells and virus-infected cells often lose their MHC-I markers, making them NK targets.

climax.text: NK cells kill by releasing proteins that punch holes in the target cell's membrane.

quiz.question: What triggers a natural killer cell to attack?
options: A cell missing its normal MHC-I marker

details.summary: Natural killer cells are innate immune lymphocytes that detect and destroy virus-infected cells and tumor cells without prior sensitization. They recognize stressed cells lacking normal surface markers and kill them by releasing cytotoxic granules that trigger cell death.
details.whyItMatters: NK cells provide rapid frontline defense against cancer and viral infections before adaptive immunity activates. Their ability to kill without prior exposure makes them critical first responders and promising candidates for cancer immunotherapy.
takeaways: NK cells kill infected and cancerous cells without needing prior exposure
They detect missing self-markers that normal cells display on their surface
NK cell therapies are being developed to treat cancers resistant to other treatments

faq.question: How do NK cells distinguish cancer cells from normal cells?
faq.answer: Normal cells display MHC class I molecules on their surface, which inhibit NK cell attack. Cancer and virus-infected cells often downregulate MHC I to hide from T cells. NK cells detect this missing self signal and kill the abnormal cell, filling a gap in immune surveillance.

faq.question: Are natural killer cells part of innate or adaptive immunity?
faq.answer: NK cells are classified as innate immune cells because they respond immediately without needing prior sensitization. However, recent research shows they can develop memory-like properties after certain infections, blurring the traditional line between innate and adaptive immunity.
